topic.km: ផ្នែកទី ១ សេចក្តីផ្តើមនៃនីតិអន្តរជាតិសាធារណៈ
topic.en: Part 1: Introduction to Public International Law

title.km: ថ្នាក់ប្រចាំសប្តាហ៍ ១

note.km: ស្លាយខាងឆ្វេងជាស្លាយដើម សង្ខេបខាងស្តាំសរសេរដោយ RoboCL។
note.en: The slide on the left is the original; the summary on the right is written by RoboCL.

slides.km: ទិដ្ឋភាពទូទៅ
slides.summary: Opens the topic with what public international law is: the body of rules, principles and standards that govern relations between states, and between states and other actors in the international community. It also flags the long-running argument over whether international law is really law, since it is built mainly on consent between sovereign states.

slides.km: ដែនកំណត់ និងបញ្ហាប្រឈម
slides.summary: Why international law is not like domestic law: there is no global legislature and no central government above states, so it works through consent (state agreement), reciprocity and self-help rather than a police force. This is the classic objection that international law is weak, and the slide sets out the limits that follow from it.

slides.km: សភាវៈនៃនីតិអន្តរជាតិ
slides.summary: Introduces the debate about the nature of international law and the different positions scholars have taken: some argue it is fundamentally different from domestic law because it lacks central enforcement, others that it is still law because states treat it as binding.

slides.km: លក្ខណៈសំខាន់ៗ
slides.summary: Lists the features that define public international law: it is a consent-based system, a horizontal system between equals (no superior authority), it relies on decentralised enforcement, and it is becoming more institutionalised through international organisations.

slides.km: វិសាលភាព និងមុខងារ
slides.summary: Shows how far international law now reaches. Once mainly about war and diplomacy, it now covers peace and security, international trade, human rights and many other fields, and its scope keeps growing as states cooperate on more subjects.

slides.km: មុខងារចម្បងៗ
slides.summary: Sets out what international law actually does: keeping peace and security between states, regulating trade and development, protecting human rights, and providing ways to settle disputes. The functions are listed one by one with the rules that carry them.

slides.km: ទំនាក់ទំនងរវាងនីតិអន្តរជាតិ និងច្បាប់ក្នុងស្រុក
slides.summary: The relationship between international law and domestic (national) law: how international rules get recognised and applied inside a state's own legal system, how courts use them, and why this matters for enforcing the law and protecting rights.

slides.km: ឯកនិយម (Monism)
slides.summary: Monism: international law and domestic law form a single legal system, so international law can become part of domestic law automatically, without a separate act of transformation. Treaties and customary rules may be applied directly by courts, and can prevail over conflicting domestic law, as in the Netherlands and France.

slides.km: ទ្វិនិយម (Dualism)
slides.summary: Dualism: international law and domestic law are two separate legal systems, different in their sources and their subjects, so an international rule needs to be transformed or incorporated by the state before a domestic court can apply it.

slides.km: វិធីសាស្ត្រចម្រុះ (Mixed)
slides.summary: In practice most states do not follow pure monism or pure dualism. They adopt mixed or hybrid approaches, applying some international rules directly and requiring transformation for others, and the choice often depends on the subject matter.

slides.km: សារៈសំខាន់ចំពោះកម្ពុជា និងអាស៊ាន
slides.en: Why it matters for Cambodia and ASEAN
slides.summary: What international law means for Cambodia and the region: regional cooperation and integration through ASEAN, participation in treaties, and the way international obligations shape domestic law and institutions.

slides.km: សារៈសំខាន់ (ត)
slides.summary: Continues the point: even without a global authority that can enforce rules against a state, international law still constrains governments in practice and gives smaller states like Cambodia a framework and a voice they would not otherwise have.

slides.km: ការវិវត្តនៃច្បាប់អន្តរជាតិ
slides.summary: Opens the history section: how international law developed over the centuries, from early practice between states through to the modern system, and the periods historians usually divide that story into.

slides.km: សន្តិភាពវេស្តហ្វាលី
slides.summary: The modern starting point is usually traced to the 17th century and the Peace of Westphalia, which is treated as marking the birth of the sovereign-state system: states as equals, each with authority inside its own territory, and no superior power above them.

slides.km: សតវត្សរ៍ទី១៩
slides.summary: International law grew quickly in the 19th century, driven by the expansion of global trade and travel, the end of colonialism in some regions, and new attempts to codify rules, including the Hague Peace Conferences and the beginnings of arbitration.

slides.km: សមាគមប្រជាជាតិ (League of Nations)
slides.summary: After the First World War, states created the League of Nations, the first attempt at a general political organisation to keep peace and manage disputes. The slide covers what it was meant to do and how it worked in practice.

slides.km: អង្គការសហប្រជាជាតិ
slides.summary: After the Second World War the international community built the United Nations in 1945, with a wider mandate: peace and security, human rights, development, and a permanent institutional framework that still shapes international law today.

slides.km: ក្រោយសង្គ្រាមត្រជាក់
slides.summary: The end of the Cold War around 1990 marked another turning point: new courts and tribunals, a stronger role for human rights and international criminal law, and more room for the Security Council to act.

slides.km: ប្រភពនៃនីតិអន្តរជាតិ
slides.summary: Introduces the sources of international law: where the rules come from, and the processes through which they are created and recognised as binding. This is the framework the following slides fill in one source at a time.

slides.km: សន្ធិសញ្ញា
slides.summary: Treaties (international conventions): written agreements between states, or between states and international organisations, that create binding obligations. The slide covers what a treaty is and the basic rules on how one is made, including signature and ratification.

slides.km: នីតិទំនៀមទម្លាប់អន្តរជាតិ
slides.summary: Customary international law grows out of the consistent and general practice of states followed out of a sense of legal obligation (opinio juris), rather than from a written text. The slide explains how custom forms and why it binds even states that never signed anything.

slides.km: គោលការណ៍ទូទៅនៃច្បាប់
slides.summary: General principles of law recognised by civilised nations are another source, used to fill gaps where neither a treaty nor custom covers the point. Examples include good faith and fairness of procedure.

slides.km: សេចក្តីសម្រេចរបស់តុលាការ
slides.summary: Judicial decisions and the writings of the most highly qualified publicists are subsidiary means for finding what the law is, not sources that create it. The slide explains the role of courts such as the ICJ and how their reasoning is used.

slides.km: ច្បាប់ទន់ (Soft Law)
slides.summary: Closing point: states also cooperate through non-binding declarations and statements from international organisations and conferences. These are not treaties and create no formal obligations, but they can still influence state behaviour and later harden into law.
